article_title: Evaluation of the Teacher Potential Project
citation: Dolfin, S., Richman, S., Choi, J., Streke, A., DeSaw, C., Demers, A., & Poznyak, D. (2019). Evaluation of the Teacher Potential Project. Washington, DC: Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/evaluation-of-the-teacher-potential-project
title: Curriculum-embedded professional development: pairing a standards-aligned curriculum with professional development for teachers
description: This design pattern embeds teacher professional development within adoption of a standards-aligned curriculum, so teachers learn practices while enacting the curriculum materials. TPP pairs "an English language arts standards-aligned curriculum and embedded professional development for teachers", and the evaluation found positive impacts on teachers' instructional practices and, after two years, on student ELA achievement.
requirements: A standards-aligned curriculum and professional development embedded in teachers' ongoing participation in the program
constraints: The evaluated student achievement impact emerged after two years of teacher participation, not after one
target_learners: Novice and experienced K-12 teachers
target_learning_goals: Common Core-aligned English language arts instructional practices
examples: TPP teachers received the EL Education ELA curriculum with embedded professional development, and were compared with teachers using district-provided curriculum and district professional development.
key_sources: Dolfin, S., Richman, S., Choi, J., Streke, A., DeSaw, C., Demers, A., & Poznyak, D. (2019). Evaluation of the Teacher Potential Project. Washington, DC: Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/evaluation-of-the-teacher-potential-project

article_title: An Experimental Evaluation of Four Elementary School Math Curricula
citation: Roberto Agodini, Barbara Harris. (2010). An Experimental Evaluation of Four Elementary School Math Curricula. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, vol. 3, no. 3. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/an-experimental-evaluation-of-four-elementary-school-math-curricula
title: Curriculum choice as a lever for early-grade math achievement gains
description: The article treats the selection among comprehensive elementary math curricula as a school-level design decision with measurable achievement consequences: switching curricula changed an average first-grader's math percentile rank by "9 to 12 points" in its estimates. The pattern is choosing a demonstrably more effective curriculum package rather than altering instruction within an existing one. It operates at the whole-curriculum grain, affecting the year's math instruction as a unit.
requirements: School must be choosing among the curricula evaluated (or similarly structured comprehensive math curricula)
constraints: The estimated advantage applies to first-grade math as reported in this evaluation
target_learners: First-grade students in elementary schools
target_learning_goals: Early-grade mathematics achievement
examples: The evaluation estimated that a school using Math Expressions or Saxon instead of Investigations or SFAW would raise an average first-grader's math percentile rank by 9 to 12 points
key_sources: Roberto Agodini, Barbara Harris. (2010). An Experimental Evaluation of Four Elementary School Math Curricula. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, vol. 3, no. 3. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/an-experimental-evaluation-of-four-elementary-school-math-curricula

article_title: Increasing parental involvement of English language learner families: What the research says
citation: Beth Tarasawa, Jacqueline Waggoner. (2015). Increasing parental involvement of English language learner families: What the research says. Journal of Children and Poverty, 21(2), 129–134. https://epsl.asu.edu/epru/documents/EPSL-0801-250-EPRU.pdf
title: Increase ELL parental involvement through both traditional and nontraditional family engagement implemented in culturally and linguistically appropriate practices
description: The brief recommends that schools seeking to increase ELL parental involvement implement "both traditional and nontraditional approaches to family engagement" within practices that are culturally and linguistically appropriate. It argues this dual approach is needed because schools often struggle to meet ELL students' instructional and linguistic needs and because parent communication barriers differ from those of mainstream families. The brief presents this as its central recommendation, supported by its research overview and illustrated by a district case study.
requirements: Practices must be culturally and linguistically appropriate to the families served
constraints: Schools often struggle to meet the unique instructional and linguistic needs of ELL students
target_learners: English language learner students and their families
target_learning_goals: Increased parental involvement in children's education
examples: The brief concludes with a case study of one public school district's successful outreach efforts implementing such engagement.

article_title: engage2learn
citation: engage2learn (e2L): Evidence Rating. (2022). https://www.evidenceforlearning.org
title: Partner districts with coaching providers that customize job-embedded professional learning to district priorities and align educator growth with learner outcomes
description: The article's program model is that e2L "partners with public schools to provide competency-focused, evidence-based coaching and job-embedded support for educators and administrators", customizing "to each partner district's specific needs and priorities". Professional learning is used to align educator growth with learner outcomes directly, rather than delivering generic training. The two matched studies linking e2L coaching to student achievement gains support this principle at a moderate evidence level.
requirements: District partnership to identify specific needs and priorities
Job-embedded coaching rather than standalone workshops
constraints: Evidence comes from two matched studies in 6th-8th grade settings in a large urban Texas district; the summary reports conflicting STAAR results in the first study
target_learners: educators and administrators in partner public school districts
target_learning_goals: improving instructional quality
improving student achievement outcomes
examples: e2L partnered with a large urban Texas district to coach 169 teachers across 10 schools during 2021-2022, and ran a second propensity-score-matched study with a second cohort of e2L teachers.
key_sources: engage2learn (e2L): Evidence Rating. (2022). https://www.evidenceforlearning.org

article_title: Family Playbook: Centering Student Voice and Experience
citation: UChicago Consortium on School Research. (2026). Family playbook: Centering student voice and experience. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/events-and-resources
title: Keep student experience survey data internal for reflection and improvement rather than public reporting or evaluation
description: The playbook presents Cultivate as "a tool for understanding and continuous improvement, not evaluation". To create the trust and space needed for honest student feedback and meaningful adult-student partnership, "Cultivate data are used internally by schools for reflection and improvement, rather than for public reporting or evaluation." The data are informational, with no thresholds to meet; lower-scoring Learning Conditions are candidates for inquiry and improvement rather than accountability targets.
requirements: A safe environment for teachers to be curious and reflective about their practice
Framing lower scores as inquiry opportunities rather than thresholds to meet
constraints: The data are not intended for comparing scores across schools, since students may choose similar responses based on very different experiences
target_learners: Students in grades 5-12
target_learning_goals: Honest student feedback and meaningful adult-student partnership to strengthen learning environments
examples: Cultivate Survey results are not public and are not used for evaluation or accountability; schools use reports after fall and spring administrations to set improvement priorities.

article_title: Portraits in Progress: Emerging Future-Ready Skills Assessment Strategies
citation: Kyle Dunbar, Katie Wilczak, Kelly Mills, Nick Mireles, and Alison Shell. (2025). Portraits in Progress: Emerging Future-Ready Skills Assessment Strategies. Digital Promise and Pearson. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Curriculum-embedded classroom activities and assessments with frequent scoring (Ephrata)
description: Teacher-designed activities embedded in the curriculum can serve as assessments of Portrait of a Graduate skills. In Ephrata Area School District, teachers develop or select six assignments per marking period that elicit evidence of skills and dispositions, rate work as recognizing, understanding, or applying the skill, and enter scores in the student information system. The report states this provides a breadth of data across settings and tasks over time, though assignment variability makes it hard to claim each scored assignment is individually valid.

constraints: Variability in the types and quality of assignments teachers use may undermine claims that each scored assignment is individually a valid assessment

examples: Ephrata's system is part of a larger assessment system including cornerstone projects and a Life Ready Graduate Certificate

article_title: College Prep for All? What We've Learned from Chicago's Efforts
citation: Elaine Allensworth, Takako Nomi, Nicholas Montgomery, & Valerie E. Lee. (2008). College Preparatory Curriculum for All: Consequences of Ninth-Grade Course Taking in Algebra and English on Academic Outcomes in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu
title: Conceptual model of curriculum-policy effects flowing through the school's instructional program
description: The article proposes a conceptual model in which a curricular policy mandate affects student outcomes only through changes in the school's instructional program: "the courses, content, and pedagogy that students receive". Enrollment depends on both program structure and student background; courses plus student response shape ninth-grade learning, which should then propagate to later achievement and post-secondary outcomes. The model guided the study's proximal (end of Grade 9) and distal (end of high school, college) outcome measures.
requirements: Beneficial effects require that schools' instructional programs adjust to the policy as expected and that students respond with better freshman-year performance
constraints: The article states some schools may have difficulty enacting substantial instructional changes, and students who would otherwise take remedial classes may not respond as expected
target_learners: first-time ninth graders in urban public high schools
target_learning_goals: college-preparatory mathematics and English coursework and subsequent academic outcomes
examples: The study measured 15 student-level outcomes at ninth grade and end of high school, mapped onto the model's proximal and distal pathways

article_title: Supporting California's Children through a Whole Child Approach: A Field Guide for Creating Integrated, School-Based Systems of Care
citation: Breaking Barriers, California Alliance of Child and Family Services, Santa Clara County Office of Education, & WestEd. (2022). Supporting California's children through a whole child approach: A field guide for creating integrated, school-based systems of care. https://WestEd.org/permissions
title: Build staff capacity for culturally responsive, asset-based family engagement
description: The guide holds that serving the whole child requires school staff equipped to build strong family partnerships through a culturally responsive approach sensitive to each family's lived experiences. "When schools put children and families first and leverage students' individual lived experiences, cultures, and languages, they strengthen the resilience of students and communities, create a culture of belonging, and maximize protective factors associated with well-being." It directs districts to the Dual Capacity-Building Framework, which offers guidance rather than prescribing specific actions.

constraints: The Dual Capacity-Building Framework does not prescribe specific actions schools must take
target_learners: Historically underserved students and families, including Filipino-American, Latino, and LGBTQ communities named in the Solano County example
target_learning_goals: Student well-being, belonging, resilience, and achievement through strong family–school partnerships
examples: Solano County's ICCTM used pláticas y conocimiento—conversations and awareness about mental health among families with similar lived experiences—and the Cultural Game Changers workforce pipeline strategy

article_title: Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems
citation: Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems. Council of Chief State School Officers. https://www.ccsso.org
title: Curriculum-embedded performance tasks contributing a substantial share of summative scores
description: Curriculum-embedded performance tasks are conducted during the school year, extend over days or weeks, and are scored with common rubrics; several can be combined into a summative score or paired with an end-of-year test. Internationally, such tasks "typically comprise 30-60 percent of the total score". In the GCSE English exam, through-course assessments "count for 60 percent of the total score; the remainder is from a written exam". The paper notes students and teachers do not experience these tasks as formal tests because they are embedded in instruction.
requirements: States or districts need to put aside professional development time for scoring the tasks; moderation or auditing systems assure comparability of teacher scoring
constraints: The paper notes these tasks should not be thought of as part of testing time but as part of teaching and learning time
target_learners: secondary students in state and national examination systems
target_learning_goals: research, inquiry, writing, and presentation of findings in content areas
examples: GCSE English classroom assessments in reading, imaginative writing, and speaking and listening; the GCSE ICT controlled assessment; Connecticut's acid rain science task; Victoria, Australia practical tasks

article_title: Design Principles for Instructionally Relevant Assessment Systems
citation: Badrinarayan, A. (2024). Design principles for instructionally relevant assessment systems. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/111.528
title: Design state assessments to be connected to and informed by high-quality curriculum
description: The Curriculum-Anchored principle argues against "curriculum agnostic" assessment design. The report states that assessments aligned only to the letter of standards, "without attending to how students developed those ideas and practices, often result in superficial assessments that are not particularly useful to any high-quality curriculum context." Instead, states should design assessments that signal, incentivize, and support high-quality instructional materials, either closely reflecting specific materials or coherently complementing them through extended transfer opportunities.
requirements: Attention to how students developed the ideas and practices being assessed, not just end-of-instruction performance
constraints: Requires states to pay more attention to and support local curriculum decisions, implying a partnership role for state education agencies
target_learners: K-12 students using high-quality instructional materials
target_learning_goals: Deeper learning through coherent curriculum-assessment alignment
Trustworthy assessment results
examples: A growing number of states provide guidance, financial incentives, and requirements for adoption and implementation of high-quality instructional materials
key_sources: Badrinarayan, A. (2024). Design principles for instructionally relevant assessment systems. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/111.528

article_title: Design Principles for Teacher Preparation: Enacting the Science of Learning and Development
citation: Darling-Hammond, L., Hyler, M. E., & Wojcikiewicz, S. (with Rushing, J.). (2025). Design principles for teacher preparation: Enacting the science of learning and development. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/115.854
title: Root teacher preparation curriculum in a deep understanding of learners, learning, and development
description: The report holds that a curriculum rooted in a deep understanding of learners, learning, and development is the most important foundation teacher preparation programs can offer, ensuring candidates have the knowledge and skills to teach and support children well. Programs should model learning rooted in culture, experience, and relationships and equip educators to understand interrelated conditions for optimal brain development. This includes a curriculum that connects subject matter with strategies for an asset-based approach to learning about students' backgrounds, families, and communities.
requirements: Knowledge of all aspects of child and adolescent development, including brain development; pedagogical content knowledge and pedagogical learner knowledge; and language development including academic language
target_learners: Teacher candidates
target_learning_goals: Understanding child and adolescent development
Adapting curriculum and assessment for individual students
examples: Programs should prepare educators who evaluate, modify, and adapt curricular materials for individual students and create assessment experiences that allow students to learn deeply through relevant inquiry

article_title: If You Listen, We Will Stay: Why Teachers of Color Leave and How to Disrupt Teacher Turnover
citation: Davis Dixon, Ashley Griffin, and Mark Teoh. (2019). If You Listen, We Will Stay: Why Teachers of Color Leave and How to Disrupt Teacher Turnover. The Education Trust & Teach Plus. https://edtrust.org
title: Create culturally affirming school environments whose goals and values align with those of teachers of color
description: Case-study principals retain teachers of color by aligning school vision with teachers' personal values: a whole-child focus, community service expectations, positive racial identity development, and equity commitments. The report found "teachers of color stay in schools that have a commitment to equity, social justice, and the dismantling of racism." Leaders set this culture through their own mindset, language, and staff-wide conversations about racism and bias.
requirements: School leaders must model and message a genuine belief in the promise of students of color, since the principal's mindset trickles down to teachers and students.
constraints: The report cautions these recommendations "may seem straightforward" but the educator voices make clear "how difficult they are to put into practice."
target_learners: K-12 teachers of color
target_learning_goals: Teacher retention and workforce diversity
examples: One school implemented mandatory weekly 45-minute "cultural proficiency seminars" where teachers have candid conversations about race and bias; another principal revised the whole PD plan around teacher-expressed needs.
key_sources: Davis Dixon, Ashley Griffin, and Mark Teoh. (2019). If You Listen, We Will Stay: Why Teachers of Color Leave and How to Disrupt Teacher Turnover. The Education Trust & Teach Plus. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED603193

article_title: AI AI Tell Me: A Model Study on the Effect of Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Feedback on Intonation in Violin Education
citation: Yakup Aksoy. (2026). Yapay zekâ, yapay zekâ söyle bana: Keman eğitiminde yapay zekâ destekli geri bildirimin entonasyona etkisine yönelik bir model çalışması. Online Journal of Music Sciences, 11(2). https://doi.org/10.31811/ojomus.1897062
title: AI-assisted intonation feedback model: Cubase cent measurement analyzed by ChatGPT and DeepSeek without teacher intervention
description: A four-week feedback pipeline in which students' violin performances were recorded with Cubase Pro 8 and the VariAudio module yielded cent-level deviation data for 44 target notes, entered manually into an intonation deviation table. Per the abstract, "Bu veriler, öğretmen müdahalesi olmaksızın ChatGPT ve DeepSeek yapay zekâ sistemleri tarafından analiz edilerek değerlendirilmiş ve öğrencilere teknik ile müzikal boyutta öneriler sunulmuştur." Students presented the table to the models via their own smartphones with a fixed prompt asking the AI to evaluate like a teacher, then planned their individual practice from the weekly feedback.
requirements: Access to Cubase software and audio recording equipment (AKG C411 microphone, RME Babyface Pro sound card)
students' personal smartphones and AI accounts
constraints: No teacher intonation feedback was given during the process; students were asked not to use vibrato; the étude was performed at 40 bpm
target_learners: music teacher candidates (violin majors, ages 19–24)
target_learning_goals: intonation accuracy in violin performance
examples: In the study, 2208 note data points were collected across the four-week application, and feedback texts were collected after each lesson as qualitative data

article_title: The Main Barrier to AI Adoption in the Public Sector is Lack of Training
citation: Vinicius Santana Gomes. (2026). The Main Barrier to AI Adoption in the Public Sector Is Lack of Training: How a Structured Method Accompanied Productivity Gains in Two Brazilian Government Cases. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01517
title: Custom AI assistants with curated legal knowledge bases, queried in de-identified form
description: The method's operational key tool in both units was a custom AI built on free-tier platform functionality (Projects in ChatGPT and Claude, Gems in Gemini) loaded with the unit's applicable normative base. As the article describes it, "By loading into the custom AI the normative base and the correct documents pertinent to the unit’s subject matter, the public servant obtains answers anchored in that base, with persona and tone configured for the institutional context." At SES/CONT the base comprised ten legal instruments (decrees, normative instructions, laws, manuals); at UCI/SEDET, modular custom AIs were built per recurring subject (e.g., Public Procurement under Law No. 14.133/2021). Queries were made de-identified, under a Data Anonymization Protocol, so submitted content ceases to be personal data under Article 12 of the Brazilian Data Protection Law.
requirements: A curated documentary/normative knowledge base pertinent to the unit's subject matter, loaded into the custom AI before use.
constraints: Queries must be de-identified: no names, case numbers, or identifiable data of the concrete case enter the tool; conversation-training features are deactivated and temporary conversation modes used.
target_learners: Public servants producing legal and technical administrative documents in internal control units
target_learning_goals: Drafting legally grounded documents, answering normative questions, and standardizing technical writing without exposing protected data
examples: SES/CONT's custom AI loaded ten legal instruments including Decree 39.701/2019 and Complementary Law 840/2011; UCI/SEDET built modular custom AIs per subject, migrated from Gemini Gems to Claude Projects.
key_sources: Vinicius Santana Gomes. (2026). The Main Barrier to AI Adoption in the Public Sector Is Lack of Training: How a Structured Method Accompanied Productivity Gains in Two Brazilian Government Cases. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01517

article_title: Studying Circular Motion with an AI-Generated Smartphone Physics Lab
citation: Josep Ll. Suñer, Francisco M. Muñoz-Pérez, Juan C. Castro-Palacio, Juan A. Monsoriu, Martín Monteiro, Cecilia Stari, and Arturo C. Martí. (2026). Uniform and Accelerated Circular Motion with a Smartphone: A No-Code, AI-Generated Browser Laboratory. https://smartphysics.webs.upv.es/rotation-lab
title: Customize laboratory software to eliminate distracting features and focus student attention exclusively on the relevant variables
description: The article states that the pedagogical value of the activity lies in software customization: instructors can eliminate distracting features common in commercial software, such as complex calibration menus or unneeded sensor channels, and focus student attention exclusively on the relevant variables (θ and ω). AI-generated applications make this customization practical without programming skills, in contrast to precompiled sensor apps whose interfaces cannot be tailored to a specific activity.

constraints: The article notes most existing smartphone experiments rely on precompiled sensor apps whose interfaces cannot be tailored to a specific activity
target_learners: introductory physics students
target_learning_goals: attending to the relevant variables of a rotational motion experiment
examples: In the reported activity the interface displays only orientation angles and angular velocity components, with only azimuth and its corresponding component taking significant values

article_title: Artificial intelligence assisted design of a novel cooperative learning technique for higher education
citation: Özgür Tutal. (2026). Artificial intelligence assisted design of a novel cooperative learning technique for higher education. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-50770-1
title: Curriculum Concept Constellation Technique (CCCT)
description: CCCT is a cooperative learning technique in which small heterogeneous groups of 4–5 students map key curriculum concepts as "stars" into visual "constellations" using metaphors. It uses a "Metaphorical and visual approach" in which "The CCCT uses the metaphor of stars forming constellations in the night sky to represent key concepts in curriculum development." Students take roles (Star Finder, Constellation Designer, Metaphor Maker, Visual Artist, Navigator) ensuring individual accountability and positive interdependence, work over two weeks, and close with a gallery walk and reflection/group processing.
requirements: Small heterogeneous groups of 4–5 members with assigned roles; simple materials (canvas, markers, sticky notes); a two-session format within a theoretical course
constraints: Designed for abstract theoretical course content without a practical component; implemented over two weeks in a curriculum development course
target_learners: sophomore prospective teachers in higher education
target_learning_goals: understanding the theoretical foundations of curriculum development
cooperative regulation of learning
positive attitudes toward cooperativeness
examples: Groups identified 5–7 key concepts such as John Dewey's philosophy, behaviorism, societal needs and developmental psychology, connected them into constellations, and described relationships with metaphors such as behaviorism as a gravitational force pulling ideas toward measurable outcomes.

article_title: Did Alice Do Wrong? Cross-Cultural Differences in Student Perceptions of Generative AI Use in University Computing Education
citation: Brian Harrington, Irina Zlotnikova, Gayathri Nadarajan, and Samuel Ekundayo. (2025). Did Alice Do Wrong? Cross-Cultural Differences in Student Perceptions of Generative AI Use in University Computing Education. ACM Trans. Comput. Educ. 26, 1, Article 15. https://doi.org/10.1145/3776558
title: Develop explicit, culturally responsive GenAI usage policies rather than relying on formal regulations alone
description: The article argues that because cultural frameworks, not formal regulations alone, shape students' ethical judgments of GenAI use, institutions should establish governance frameworks that are "both culturally responsive and ethically sound." Recommended measures include explicit GenAI usage policies clarifying distinctions between acceptable assistance and unauthorized content generation, culturally sensitive AI literacy programs, and regular review of academic integrity codes with specific GenAI guidance. The principle rests on the finding that identical policies produced different judgments across cultural contexts.
requirements: Institutional governance frameworks that reflect cultural differences in perceptions of collaboration, authority, and academic integrity
constraints: AI tools themselves often reflect culturally embedded biases, complicating universal ethical frameworks, as the authors caution citing prior work
target_learners: university students in computing education
higher education institutions across diverse cultural contexts
target_learning_goals: responsible and ethical use of generative AI in coursework
academic integrity understanding
examples: The study's two surveyed institutions had functionally identical GenAI policies yet students' judgments differed systematically by country, motivating the call for culturally tailored guidelines
key_sources: Brian Harrington, Irina Zlotnikova, Gayathri Nadarajan, and Samuel Ekundayo. (2025). Did Alice Do Wrong? article_title: CourseGraph: Finding overlaps and differences in Computer Science courses across universities
citation: Arthur Nijdam, Paul Stankovski Wagner, Sara Ramezanian. (2026). CourseGraph: Finding overlaps and differences in Computer Science courses across universities. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05910
title: Administrator decision process for external-course credit as a model of overlap assessment criteria (RQ1)
description: The article models how curriculum assessors decide whether an external course can be credited: scope classification (in-program vs external, with a 15 ECTS external cap), matching to a home course, level assignment (basic G1, intermediate G2, advanced A), specialization-track membership, and proportional crediting of partial overlap. The authors summarize that "the content and level of the course needs to be appropriate for a course to be counted as part of the degree program." CourseGraph operationalizes the content-overlap portion of this model, emulating the first and third decisions of the administrator's process.
requirements: Access to curriculum metadata such as mandatory-course lists and specialization-track contents
constraints: The paper focuses on content overlap; automatic level assignment is left to future implementation
target_learners: university program administrators and exchange students
target_learning_goals: consistent, scalable assessment of external courses for degree credit
examples: The five C-program specialization tracks (KS, PVS, PVT, SEC, ADV) illustrate track-membership classification
key_sources: Arthur Nijdam, Paul Stankovski Wagner, Sara Ramezanian. (2026). CourseGraph: Finding overlaps and differences in Computer Science courses across universities. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05910

article_title: Educational Organizations in the AI Era: Digital Management and Leadership, Digital Skills, and Innovation
citation: Gerasimos Kalogeratos, Eleni Anastasopoulou, Triada Kapota. (2026). Educational Organizations in the AI Era: Digital Management and Leadership, Digital Skills, and Innovation. International Journal of Advanced Multidisciplinary Research and Studies. https://doi.org/10.62225/2583049X.2026.6.3.6209
title: Cultivate an innovation-oriented organizational culture that encourages experimentation, adaptability, and knowledge sharing
description: Because AI integration succeeds or fails on human and organizational capacity, educational organizations should foster a culture oriented toward continuous innovation. article_title: Empowerment over enforcement: unpacking the psychological drivers of AI-assisted deep revision in EFL writing
citation: Li, H. and Zhang, W. (2026). Empowerment over enforcement: unpacking the psychological drivers of AI-assisted deep revision in EFL writing. Front. Psychol. 17:1871022. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1871022
title: Cultivate AI prompting literacy and autonomy-supportive environments rather than relying on monitoring-based mandates
description: Because APL significantly predicted the psychological needs and DRE while External Mandate showed a negligible direct path, the article recommends that policies "prioritize the cultivation of students' prompting literacy and the creation of a psychologically safe, autonomy-supportive environment." Educators are encouraged to re-evaluate monitoring-centric policies obsessed with usage metrics or AI-detection software, pivot to AI prompting workshops, and let formative feedback take precedence over summative assessment.

article_title: Curiosity as Linguistic Intervention: Using LLM Tutoring Dialogues to Influence Exploratory Learning Behavior
citation: Ganganath, G., Bolonghege, P., Lyu, Q., Varakantham, P., & Kandappu, T. (2026). Curiosity as Linguistic Intervention: Using LLM Tutoring Dialogues to Influence Exploratory Learning Behavior. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22349
title: CURIOBOT curiosity-modulated tutoring framework
description: CURIOBOT is an inference-time prompting framework that turns Berlyne's collative variables into five conversational operators — NOVELTY, COMPLEXITY, CONFLICT, UNCERTAINTY, and NEUTRAL — selected adaptively at each tutor turn from interaction signals such as response depth and learner initiative. COMPLEXITY "expands the surrounding conceptual space by exposing additional mechanisms and dependencies" while the intervention modifies only conversational framing, keeping the topic and learning objective unchanged. Both operator selection and response generation are implemented with prompted black-box LLMs without fine-tuning.
requirements: A shared system prompt defining the tutoring role, plus operator-conditioned generation separated from a modulator stage that analyzes dialogue context before each tutor turn
constraints: The Modulator is a prompted LLM agent with a fixed decision rule, leaving the operator-selection policy itself unoptimized, per the article's limitations section
target_learners: Postgraduate students learning topics in STEM, social sciences, and arts & humanities
target_learning_goals: Exploratory questioning, conversational agency, productive struggle, and observable epistemic curiosity during tutoring dialogue
examples: In the 3×3×3 factorial study, each domain was assigned to one tutoring variant (Baseline, CURIOBOT, or study-oriented mode), producing 270 conversations across Claude, Gemini, and GPT

An AI-Powered Culturally Aware Chatbot for Stress Detection and Wellness Support among Pakistani University Students Using NLP and Machine Learning. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=An+AI-Powered+Culturally+Aware+Chatbot+for+Stress+Detection+and+Wellness+Support+among+Pakistani+University+Students

description: The principle is to encode cultural specificity in the system prompt that steers the language model, rather than relying on a general-purpose chatbot. Knowledge of the target population's culturally specific stressors and preferred languages of distress expression

students in South Asian contexts underserved by Western-designed mental health tools

Willingness to engage with mental health support despite stigma that deters open sharing

citation: Jiayi Wang, Ruiwei Xiao, Xinying Hou, Hanqi Li, Ying Jui Tseng, John Stamper, and Ken Koedinger. (2025). LLMs to Support K–12 Teachers in Culturally Relevant Pedagogy: An AI Literacy Example. https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.08083

It combines "demographic characteristics of the students, rubric-based feedback, and just-in-time coaching" and offers two tiers of lesson modifications, basic and advanced, based on a CRT checklist, plus an interactive chatbot simulating instructional coaching.

article_title: K12-KGraph: A Curriculum-Aligned Knowledge Graph for Benchmarking and Training Educational LLMs
citation: Hao Liang, Qihan Lin, Mingrui Chen, Hengyi Feng, Zhaoyang Han, Xiaochen Ma, Zhen Hao Wong, Meiyi Qiang, Linzhuang Sun, Wentao Zhang. (2026). K12-KGraph: A Curriculum-Aligned Knowledge Graph for Benchmarking and Training Educational LLMs. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09635
title: Curriculum cognition: structured understanding of how knowledge is organized and visually presented
description: The article names curriculum cognition as the construct that existing benchmarks fail to test and current instruction-tuning data fails to teach. It defines it as "the structured understanding of how knowledge is organized and visually presented, including prerequisite chains, concept taxonomies, experiment-concept links, and pedagogical sequencing." A competent teacher knows not only that a topic exists but what it requires as prerequisites, where it sits in the taxonomy, and where in the textbook it first appears. The K12-KGraph resources are designed to measure and teach this construct.
requirements: Probing it requires benchmark items derived from curriculum structure (prerequisites, taxonomy, location) rather than factual recall questions
constraints: Operationalized for the Chinese K-12 People's Education Press curriculum across mathematics, physics, chemistry, and biology
target_learners: K-12 students in Chinese primary, middle, and high school
target_learning_goals: Understanding prerequisite chains, concept taxonomies, experiment-concept links, and pedagogical sequencing
examples: The article illustrates the construct with a 7th-grade mathematics teacher knowing that linear equations requires arithmetic operations as a prerequisite and first appears in Chapter 3 of the textbook

article_title: The Easy Trap: Why LLMs Underestimate Misconception-Driven Difficulty
citation: La Hadi, A., Alibasa, M. J., Chen, G., & Asyhari, A. T. (2025). The “Easy Trap”: Why LLMs Underestimate Misconception-Driven Difficulty.
title: Curricular versus cognitive difficulty: LLMs encode instructional sequencing expectations rather than misconception-driven difficulty
description: The article distinguishes two forms of difficulty: "curricular difficulty, reflected in LLM-generated estimates based on procedural and textual features" and "cognitive difficulty, reflected in empirical performance shaped by learner misconceptions." It argues LLMs approximate what should be easy based on instructional sequencing rather than what is actually difficult due to persistent misconceptions, producing systematic underestimation of misconception-driven items — the "Easy Trap." This account explains why fraction items introduced early in curricula but conceptually conflicting are rated easy by LLMs yet prove hardest for undergraduates.
requirements: Requires empirical learner performance data (CTT p-values or IRT difficulty parameters) to contrast against model-generated difficulty estimates
constraints: Evidence comes from fraction arithmetic among Indonesian undergraduates; the article states it remains unclear whether the phenomenon appears in other mathematical domains such as algebra, geometry, or calculus
target_learners: undergraduate students in mandatory mathematics courses
target_learning_goals: accurate estimation of item difficulty for assessment design and adaptive learning systems
examples: The study compared four LLM systems' 1–100 difficulty ratings against CTT and 2PL IRT difficulty from 770 undergraduates on 32 arithmetic items

article_title: PhysicsMate: A Curriculum-Grounded Bengali Benchmark for Secondary Physics QA with Small-Model Adaptation
citation: Rashid Azraf Jahin, Saadman Sajid, Khan Raiyan Ibne Reza, Sumaiya Tabassum Nimi. (2026). PhysicsMate: A Curriculum-Grounded Bengali Benchmark for Secondary Physics QA with Small-Model Adaptation. IEEE CSDE 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00664v1
title: Curriculum-grounded ontology framework for building educational QA benchmarks
description: The article proposes an end-to-end framework in which a national curriculum textbook is ingested via OCR and semantic chunking, formalized against a predefined domain ontology, and used to construct a provenance-traced QA benchmark with category-level evaluation. Unlike prior systems that construct graphs from text, PhysicsMate "utilizes the curriculum-defined ontology to build and partition the benchmark and support the category-level evaluation". The authors argue the framework generalizes to adjacent disciplines (secondary chemistry, biology) and to neighbouring South Asian curricula sharing classical physics and SI units at Grade 9-10.
requirements: A curriculum textbook serving as the source of truth, a predefined ontology matching the domain's knowledge types, and structured extraction prompts that limit representation variability.
constraints: Humanities curricula require restructuring declarative and procedural primitives into causal, temporal and narrative relation types; generalization to other syllabi has not been tested.
target_learners: Secondary students in national-curriculum systems, particularly under-resourced regional education ecosystems in South Asia
target_learning_goals: Curriculum-aligned STEM question answering and controlled category-level model evaluation
examples: The extraction pipeline yielded 811 semantic units from three-page contextual windows with two-page overlaps, each traceable to its originating text.

article_title: AI as a cognitive partner in learning: Emerging epistemic practices of reflective thought
citation: Dalsgaard, C., & Prilop, C. N. (2026). AI as a cognitive partner in learning: Emerging epistemic practices of reflective thought. Journal of Research on Technology in Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/15391523.2026.2695013
title: Cultivate, do not ban: teach students to use AI as a mediating tool for reflective thought within process-oriented assignments
description: The article's central implication for teaching practice is "not to ban AI use, but to cultivate students' abilities to engage with AI tools as mediating tools for reflective thought". Teachers should redirect focus from products toward processes, frame AI use within examination, construction, and reflection, and show how AI supports each process differently — explanations for examination, methods when stuck in construction, and improvement suggestions for reflection. Teachers should make the processes visible, for instance through assignments where students demonstrate and reflect on cognitive partnership processes.

constraints: Risk remains that students use AI to outsource cognitive processes; the recommendation targets partnership use, not product-level outsourcing
target_learners: upper secondary school students
target_learning_goals: reflective thought, examination, construction, and reflection in subject-area work
examples: In the project, 59 teachers from eight schools developed exploratory action plans with AI-based student assignments across two five-month intervention cycles

Goal-setting and problem-solving skills are named as important augmentative skills. article_title: Game-based learning: A design-based theory of teaching–learning–assessment systems
citation: Sireci, S. G., Tucker, E. M., & Gordon, E. W. (Eds.). (2025). Handbook for Assessment in the Service of Learning, Volume II: Reconceptualizing Assessment to Improve Learning. University of Massachusetts Amherst Libraries. https://openpublishing.library.umass.edu/
title: Make assessments adaptive and culturally sustaining so human variance is leveraged rather than treated as noise
description: This principle treats learner variance in development, culture, language, and interests as an asset to be understood and leveraged rather than noise to be minimized. Gordon argues assessments "should be able to accommodate different ways of demonstrating learning and provide entry points for learners of varying skill levels (the idea of 'low floor, high ceiling' tasks)" and should be sensitive to the languages, values, prior knowledge, and identities students bring. He links this to equity, noting that when assessment is used purely as a high-stakes gatekeeper it has often exacerbated social inequalities, and that recognizing growth and multiple abilities supports positive learner identity.
requirements: Tasks with low floor and high ceiling; sensitivity to students' cultural contexts and languages; a supportive, trustful environment
constraints: The article states high-stakes gatekeeping uses of assessment have often exacerbated social inequalities, a condition this principle is meant to counter
target_learners: Culturally and linguistically diverse learners, including bilingual students
target_learning_goals: Equitable demonstration of learning, positive learner identity, growth
examples: An assessment that allows a bilingual student to draw on both languages may better capture and cultivate full communicative ability

article_title: Does Curricular Complexity in Computer Science Influence the Representation of Women CS Graduates?
citation: Albert Lionelle, McKenna Quam, Carla Brodley, and Catherine Gill. 2024. Does Curricular Complexity in Computer Science Influence the Representation of Women CS Graduates?. In Proceedings of the 55th ACM Technical Symposium on Computer Science Education V. 1 (SIGCSE 2024). https://doi.org/10.1145/3626252.3630835
title: Curricular analytics: graph-based measures of degree-program complexity (blocking, delay, centrality, structural complexity)
description: Curricular analytics is the study of academic program design and layout, in which a degree plan is translated into a directed acyclic graph of courses and prerequisites. From the graph, four measures are computed: blocking factor (the number of courses reachable from a course node), delay factor (the maximum number of courses that must be completed in sequential order), centrality (the sum of the delay of all paths containing that course), and structural complexity (an unweighted linear combination of delay and blocking, with overall program complexity the sum of individual course complexities). The article uses these measures to compare 60 CS degrees against representation of women graduates.
requirements: A degree map built from a plan of study and each course's pre- and/or co-requisites, translated into a directed acyclic graph
constraints: Delay factor does not account for course availability, terms, enrollment caps, and other real-world factors, so it should not be read as semesters to graduate; structural complexity does not evaluate course content
target_learners: Undergraduate computer science majors
target_learning_goals: On-time progression and graduation through a computing degree program
examples: For the example degree map in Figure 1, Data Structures had blocking factor 11, delay factor 6, centrality 39, and complexity 17, with overall program complexity 175

article_title: The Triumph of Users: Achieving Cultural Usability Goals With User Localization
citation: Huatong Sun. (2006). The Triumph of Users: Achieving Cultural Usability Goals With User Localization. Technical Communication Quarterly, 15(4), 457-481. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15427625tcq1504_5
title: Cultural usability framework: usability as a diffusing feature situated at the intersection of immediate and sociocultural contexts
description: The framework of cultural usability integrates key concepts and methods from activity theory, genre theory, and British cultural studies to study local use in context. It "regards usability as a diffusing feature across the activity system" and incorporates cultural factors from both the immediate context and the sociocultural context. It situates culture in the dynamic interactions of instrumental affordances (operation and action levels) and social affordances (activity level, informed by genre theory and British cultural studies), treating usability as both a material interaction with the artifact and an interpretation process.

constraints: Activity theory alone is good at interpreting tool-mediated production but weak at sign-mediated communication, which the framework supplements with genre theory and British cultural studies

article_title: Cultural differences in online learning: International student perceptions
citation: Liu, X., Liu, S., Lee, S.-h., & Magjuka, R. J. (2010). Cultural Differences in Online Learning: International Student Perceptions. Educational Technology & Society, 13(3), 177-188. https://www.jstor.org/stable/jeductechsoci.13.3
title: Design culturally inclusive online learning environments by building diversity into course design
description: The principle holds that online courses serving international students should incorporate diversity in assessment strategies, technology use and case materials so that all students can participate fully. As the article states, "a culturally inclusive learning environment needs to consider diversity in course design in order to ensure full participation by international students." The authors argue diversity is the best solution for respecting culturally different ways of learning and ensuring equity, while noting a tension between localizing instruction for particular cultures and serving a group with multiple nationalities.
requirements: Instructors need awareness of students' expectations and cultural backgrounds, e.g. through a quick learner analysis, to adjust the diversity of the course
constraints: Localization for one culture may be difficult to implement in a group with multiple nationalities without compromising the interests of students from other nations

article_title: Instructional design frameworks and intercultural models
citation: Patricia A. Young. (2009). Instructional Design Frameworks and Intercultural Models. Information Science Reference, IGI Global. http://www.igi-global.com/reference
title: Culture-Based Model (CBM): an intercultural instructional design framework for culture-based ICTs
description: CBM is an intercultural instructional design framework that assists designers, researchers, and practitioners in building culture-based ICTs. The book states that "CBM is an intercultural, instructional design framework that guides designers through the management, design, development, and assessment process while taking into account explicit culture-based considerations." CBM operates inside, outside, and across cultures, and is adaptive: it "can be used in conjunction with traditional instructional design models or on its own." It focuses broadly on the management and design processes and what the content should be, bringing the human element into design disciplines.
requirements: Designers prescribe methods on the basis of preproduction analysis and research, ongoing production, and postproduction
constraints: The book does not claim to incorporate all factors consistent with culture-based designs; it provides a comprehensive set of design factors that, when implemented, can best serve to authenticate a culture-based design
Taking full advantage of the culture-based model is dependent upon including either design experts or culture experts on the project team, per the foreword
target_learners: Instructional designers and e-learning designers
graduate and undergraduate students designing ICTs
researchers
target_learning_goals: Designing culturally responsive instructional products and online environments
analyzing cultures and defining target audiences

article_title: Instructional design frameworks and intercultural models
citation: Patricia A. Young. (2009). Instructional Design Frameworks and Intercultural Models. Information Science Reference, IGI Global. http://www.igi-global.com/reference
title: Treat culture as a core construct of all design decisions and make integrating culture an explicit act
description: The book positions culture as a design construct that has been neglected in instructional design. It argues that "Culture is a core construct of all design decisions; however, its potential to improve the design process has been mostly ignored in the field of instructional design," citing reasons such as designers not knowing how to represent culture and the absence of a framework aligning culture with ADDIE. Because designs and designers are not equitable, "Integrating culture in design must be an explicit act"—designing for people means designing with culture in mind.
requirements: Designers must acknowledge their own culture, language, ideologies, and standards, and examine situations from the point of view of the target audience
constraints: The assumption that if one thinks culture, one does culture is not true, per Scheel and Branch as cited
target_learners: Instructional designers
corporate designers working with global markets
educators serving ethnically diverse students
target_learning_goals: Making instruction accessible for diverse groups of people
avoiding imposition of designer ideologies on target audiences
examples: The preface lists situations when culture should be considered, including when learners fail to learn, when users fail to understand user interfaces, and when the design of a product fails learners or users

article_title: Integrating Culture in the Design of ICTs
citation: Patricia A. Young. (2008). Integrating Culture in the Design of ICTs. British Journal of Educational Technology, Vol 39 No 1, 6-17. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8535.2007.00699.x
title: Culture based circumference: design specifications range from generic/culture-neutral to specialised/culture-specific
description: The article proposes a 'culture based circumference' (Figure 1) as an organizing framework for integrating culture in ICT design. Both ends of the continuum are culture based: 'Generic features can be generalised across cultures but they are still culture based', while specialised features 'focus on meeting the needs of the target audience'. Internationalisation produces generic, culture-neutral designs; localisation produces specialised, culture-specific designs. The framework widens the palette designers can draw on beyond either pole alone.

constraints: The article notes this is a sampling of literature, not a complete review, and game design was excluded for space
target_learners: Designers of ICTs for diverse international and local audiences
target_learning_goals: Integrating culture deliberately in the design of information and communication technologies
examples: The article maps internationalisation to the generic pole and localisation to the specialised pole of the circumference

citation: van Kesteren, M. T. R., Rijpkema, M., Ruiter, D. J., Morris, R. G. M., & Fernández, G. (2014). Building on Prior Knowledge: Schema-dependent Encoding Processes Relate to Academic Performance. Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience, 26(10), 2250–2261. https://doi.org/10.1162/jocn_a_00630
title: Structure curricula so new material connects to students' existing conceptual schemas
description: Because activated prior conceptual schemas facilitate encoding and long-term retention of new related material, the article recommends that learning be built on well-structured prior knowledge: "Optimal construction and usage of a schema is thus recommended to lead to better structured learning." In the study, this was operationalized by constructing sentences that each contained at least one term learned in the first year of study and one new term from later courses, embedding the experiment within the actual university curriculum.
requirements: Knowledge of what conceptual schemas learners already possess, so new material can be matched to it
constraints: Benefits apply to information related to an existing schema; mismatching information relies on MTL-dependent binding instead
target_learners: university undergraduates in discipline-specific curricula
target_learning_goals: long-term acquisition and retention of conceptual disciplinary knowledge
examples: Stimulus sentences paired a first-year concept with a new concept (e.g., a known term 'excitatory neurotransmitter' with the new term 'glutamate'), and participants' grades were obtained for Study Year 1 and Study Year 2

article_title: Constructing Meaning When Reading Poetry: An Expert-Novice Study
citation: Peskin, J. (1998). Constructing meaning when reading poetry: An expert-novice study. Cognition and Instruction, 16(3), 235-263. https://doi.org/10.1207/s1532690xci1603_3
title: Culler's structuralist model of poetic communication: reading poetry is charged with artifice, governed by shared conventions of significance, thematic unity and metaphorical coherence.
description: The article adopts Jonathan Culler's structuralist model as the framework for its second research question, treating reading poetry as "not a natural activity but is charged with artifice", animated by a special set of expectations or conventions assimilated by readers and shared with the author. The primary expectations are the rule of significance (read the poem as expressing a significant attitude to some problem concerning man and/or his relation to the universe), the convention of thematic unity (all parts relate to create a unified, coherent whole), and the conventions of metaphorical coherence (the basis of poetic expression is the metaphor). The study tests whether novices show evidence of having assimilated these conventions, and finds they have.
requirements: Readers must have considerable experience with the conventions, since the study of one poem facilitates the reading of the next
constraints: The conventions impose severe limitations on the set of acceptable or plausible readings rather than guaranteeing comprehension of any particular poem
target_learners: secondary and undergraduate students reading poetry
target_learning_goals: interpreting poetry and constructing coherent readings of literary texts
examples: The study coded think-aloud protocols of eight novices for evidence of the three conventions while reading two period poems.

article_title: Conceptualizing the designs of authentic computer-supported collaborative learning environments in schools
citation: Yotam Hod, Ornit Sagy. (2019). Conceptualizing the Designs of Authentic Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning Environments in Schools. http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007%2Fs11412-019-09300-7 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09300-7
title: A three-cultures framework of authentic learning design distinguishes current, authentic, and intended cultures
description: The article proposes that every design for authenticity involves three distinct but related cultures: the current culture ("a pattern of activities that is developed over time for a community to achieve its valued purposes"), the authentic culture ("the professional or expert culture(s) that the teacher or designer wants the students to enculturate"), and the intended culture, the teacher's or designer's vision or figured world of that authentic culture. This refines Brown et al.'s bicultural classroom-versus-practitioner account by making the intended culture explicit. The review derived it through constant-comparative analysis and found it commensurate with every case examined.
requirements: Designs for authenticity must make the intended culture explicit, since the intended culture is a conceptual bridge between current classroom culture and one or more authentic cultures
constraints: All authentic cultures are current cultures under the article's definitions, but not all current cultures are authentic cultures
target_learners: students in school CSCL environments designed for authenticity
target_learning_goals: enculturation of professional or expert practices in a domain
examples: The review applied the framework to 28 cases from ijCSCL and JLS, validating it with Brown & Campione (1994) and Radinsky et al. (2001) outside the original corpus

citation: Meg Farrell, Monika Martin, Ricardo Böheim, Alexander Renkl, Werner Rieß, Karen D. Könings, Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer, Tina Seidel. (2024). Signaling cues and focused prompts for professional vision support: The interplay of instructional design and situational interest in preservice teachers' video analysis. Instructional Science (2024) 52:879–917. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09662-y
title: Use integrated keyword cueing as a fallback support when situational interest is difficult to elicit
description: The article's stated practice implication is that "keyword cueing can offer an alternative when interest is difficult to elicit". Its rationale is a moderation pattern reported in the abstract: "training with cues fostered professional vision skills for preservice teachers with low situational interest", suggesting cues "may compensate for the generative processing boost typically associated with situational interest". Designers should therefore treat situational interest as a design component first and reserve cueing for uninterested novices, since the techniques "did not generally offer additional support".

constraints: the article attributes the cue benefit only to preservice teachers with low situational interest and reports no general additional support from the techniques

target_learning_goals: professional vision noticing and reasoning during video analysis
examples: In the study's training phase, 63 participants watched cue-embedded videos while 67 watched plain versions of the same videos.

article_title: The role of metacognitive experience: Can feedback training affect kindergarteners'monitoring accuracy?
citation: Kristin Kolloff, Ebru Ger, Claudia M. Roebers. (2025). The role of metacognitive experience: Can feedback training affect kindergarteners' monitoring accuracy? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09422-4
title: Cue utilization framework combined with Efklides' multilevel metacognition model as basis for monitoring training
description: The study integrates Koriat's (1997) cue utilization approach, which holds that individuals use mnemonic heuristics such as retrieval fluency as cues to inform monitoring, with Efklides' (2008) model framing metacognitive experiences and social feedback as shaping monitoring development. The article states that "retrieval fluency typically functions as a valid mnemonic cue, and its use is consistently related to monitoring accuracy." This dual framework motivated testing whether feedback and repeated experiences help children discover and use valid task-inherent cues.
requirements: Repeated metacognitive experiences across multiple task trials for children to discover valid cues
constraints: Young children's monitoring judgments tend to be inaccurate due to underdeveloped recognition and use of valid task-inherent cues, per the framework
target_learners: kindergarten-aged children (around 6 years old)
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring accuracy
cue utilization in memory tasks
examples: The training app exposed children to varying retrieval fluency across 12 sessions of paired-associates memory tasks with confidence judgments after each recognition trial

article_title: Rubrics enhance accuracy and reduce cognitive load in self-assessment
citation: Rebecca Krebs, Björn Rothstein, Julian Roelle. (2022). Rubrics enhance accuracy and reduce cognitive load in self-assessment. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09302-1
title: Cue-utilization and offloading account of how rubrics support self-assessment
description: The article frames rubrics as documents that "provide learners with the assessment criteria and, based on these criteria, illustrate different levels of quality". Theoretically, transparent quality levels supply diagnostic cues on which learners base judgments, increasing accuracy per cue-utilization theory; the reduced perceived difficulty indicates rubrics also serve an offloading function, relieving learners from deciding which criteria apply to each quality level.
requirements: Learners must be introduced to the assessment criteria and quality levels the rubric covers
constraints: Under strict time constraints rubrics might induce stress and pressure and hinder task performance, per the article's citation of Panadero & Romero (2014)
target_learners: high school students self-assessing written scientific abstracts
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment of complex writing performance
examples: In the experiment, rubric learners rated their abstracts on six quality levels per criterion with the rubric's aspect descriptions visible, while control learners used the same scales without guidance

article_title: Curiosity can influence metacognitive processes
citation: Sunae Kim, Paul L Harris, Benjamin Néher. (2025). Curiosity can influence metacognitive processes. Metacognition and Learning (2025) 20:39. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09444-y
title: Curiosity serves a metacognitive function: a bidirectional account linking curiosity to metacognitive monitoring and control
description: The article proposes that the relationship between curiosity and metacognition is bidirectional: metacognitive experiences elicit curiosity (as prior frameworks assume), and feelings of curiosity in turn guide metacognitive monitoring and control. The authors suggest that "feelings of curiosity serve similar functions as internal heuristics, which then guide metacognitive monitoring and control", situating curiosity among internal cues such as familiarity and processing fluency. They also connect the findings to Shea and colleagues' distinction between metacognition 1 (individual level) and metacognition 2 (shared metacognitive information used to coordinate decisions), arguing that people use others' curiosity to recalibrate their own metacognitive experiences.
requirements: Curiosity must be measured or manipulated independently of information-seeking so that metacognitive functions can be distinguished from automatic curiosity-driven behavior
constraints: The exact mechanisms underlying the interplay between curiosity and metacognitive processes remain beyond the scope of the present research
Experiments 1 and 2 provide only correlational evidence; only the 3A–3B comparison directly examined the impact of curiosity on metacognitive control
Findings are from adult samples (Hungarian and UK) answering general knowledge questions
target_learners: adults answering general knowledge questions
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring of answer accuracy
metacognitive control decisions such as withholding responses

article_title: Exploring the relations between teachers’ cue-utilization, monitoring and regulation of students’ text learning
citation: Janneke van de Pol, Selia N. van den Boom-Muilenburg, Tamara van Gog. (2021). Exploring the relations between teachers' cue-utilization, monitoring and regulation of students' text learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09268-6
title: Cue-utilization framework applied to teacher monitoring of student text comprehension
description: The article organizes its study around the cue-utilization framework (Koriat, 1997), in which monitoring accuracy depends on how predictive the information, or cues, used for monitoring judgments is for students' actual performance. Teachers need "bits of information (also known as 'cues') that are predictive or diagnostic of students' comprehension". The framework distinguishes performance cues, student cues, and task cues, and predicts that more diagnostic cue availability yields more accurate monitoring and, in turn, more adaptive regulation.
requirements: Teachers must have and use cues that are predictive or diagnostic of students' comprehension for monitoring judgments to be accurate.
constraints: The article notes previous studies did not find monitoring differences between student-cues-only and student-plus-performance-cues conditions, complicating the framework's simple prediction.
target_learners: secondary education teachers
target_learning_goals: accurate monitoring of students' text comprehension
adaptive regulation of students' learning from texts
examples: Teachers judged fifteen students under three cue-availability conditions: name-only, name + diagram, and diagram-only, with task cues always available.

citation: Pijeira-Díaz, H. J., van de Pol, J., Channa, F., & de Bruin, A. (2023). Scaffolding self-regulated learning from causal-relations texts: Diagramming and self-assessment to improve metacomprehension accuracy? Metacognition and Learning, 18, 631–658. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09343-0
title: Cue-utilization framework for metacomprehension and the diagramming paradigm
description: The article works within the view that metacognitive judgments are inferential: students weight cues "in an analogous way to a multiple regression model" to predict performance. Metacomprehension accuracy depends on using cues whose diagnosticity (correlation with performance) is high; generative scaffolds such as completing pre-structured causal diagrams make diagnostic cues available before judgment. The diagramming paradigm sequences reading, diagram completion, comprehension judgments, restudy selection, and testing.
requirements: Students must complete a generative task (e.g., a pre-structured causal diagram) between reading and judging so diagnostic cues become available
constraints: Cue utilization is calculated with correlations, so causality cannot be asserted; the scaffold targets expository causal-relations texts rather than narrative texts or isolated facts

target_learning_goals: accurate monitoring of text comprehension
self-regulated restudy decisions when learning from causal-relations expository texts
examples: Students read six Dutch expository texts, completed pre-structured diagrams with four empty boxes, judged comprehension, selected texts for restudy, and took a comprehension test

article_title: Individual differences in local and global metacognitive judgments
citation: Marion Händel & Anique B. H. de Bruin & Markus Dresel (2020). Individual differences in local and global metacognitive judgments. Metacognition and Learning (2020) 15:51–75. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09220-0
title: Cue-utilization approach to metacognitive judgments
description: The article adopts Koriat's cue-utilization approach as its theoretical framework for explaining the bases and accuracy of metacognitive judgments. Judgments are inferential and rest on cues: information-based (or theory-based) cues such as self-concept beliefs and prior success, and experience-based cues such as retrieval fluency and experienced task difficulty during task processing. The article uses this framework to derive hypotheses about which predictors should matter for local versus global judgments and for predictions versus postdictions, stating that "the accuracy of judgments depends on the availability of specific cues."
requirements: Judgments are inferential and depend on the cues available to the judge at the time of judging
constraints: Local judgments can more easily draw on experience-based task-specific cues, while global judgments and predictions rely more on information-based cues such as domain-familiarity or self-concept
target_learners: undergraduate teacher education students
target_learning_goals: accurate metacognitive monitoring of test performance
examples: Study 1 and Study 2 regressed local and global judgments and accuracy scores on performance, motivational, and personality variables interpreted as information-based versus experience-based cues

article_title: What moderates the accuracy of ease of learning judgments?
citation: Jemstedt, A., Kubik, V., & Jönsson, F. U. (2017). What moderates the accuracy of ease of learning judgments? Metacognition and Learning, 12, 337–355. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-017-9172-3
title: Cue-utilization account of ease of learning judgments
description: The article adopts Koriat's (1997) cue-utilization approach, under which metacognitive judgments are inferential: people use available cues or heuristics, such as semantic relatedness, to infer how difficult material will be to learn. Because EOL judgments are made early, before idiosyncratic learning cues are available, accuracy "should mainly be based on the validity and discriminability of salient cues in the material". The experiments operationalize this by varying semantic relatedness within lists and measuring whether judgments track that cue.
requirements: Material must contain salient cues, such as semantic relatedness, that vary enough within the list to allow discrimination between items
constraints: EOL accuracy is capped by the predictive validity of the available cue for actual learnability
Idiosyncratic cues indicating how well material has been learned are largely unavailable at the pre-study stage
target_learners: undergraduate psychology students studying paired-associate material
target_learning_goals: accurate pre-study metacognitive monitoring of item difficulty to guide study decisions
examples: In Experiment 1, lists high versus low in semantic-relatedness variability produced gamma of .74 versus .21, supporting the cue-based account

article_title: The role of achievement emotions for text comprehension and metacomprehension
citation: Prinz-Weiß, A., Lukosiute, L., Meyer, M., & Riedel, J. (2023). The role of achievement emotions for text comprehension and metacomprehension. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09331-w
title: Cue-utilization framework extended to achievement emotions as metacomprehension judgment cues
description: The cue-utilization framework holds that when providing judgments, learners infer their level of comprehension based on available information, known as cues. This study extends the framework by treating state achievement emotions experienced during reading as potential judgment cues for predictions and postdictions. The findings show learners do use these emotions as cues, but the article concludes that achievement emotions "do not necessarily represent valid cues for judging comprehension", so relying on them can produce over- or underconfidence and hinder self-regulated learning from texts.
requirements: Learners must experience and be able to report state achievement emotions during the learning activity for the emotions to function as judgment cues
constraints: The article states emotions are not regularly diagnostic of actual comprehension; positive emotions were not associated with better comprehension in this study, so emotion-based judgments can impair accuracy
target_learners: senior high school students learning from texts
target_learning_goals: accurate monitoring of text comprehension
effective self-regulated learning from texts

article_title: Effects of availability of diagnostic and non-diagnostic cues on the accuracy of teachers’ judgments of students’ text comprehension
citation: Janneke van de Pol, Eleanor Rowan, Eva Janssen, Tamara van Gog. (2024). Effects of availability of diagnostic and non-diagnostic cues on the accuracy of teachers' judgments of students' text comprehension. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09383-0
title: Cue-utilization framework of metacognitive monitoring applied to teacher judgment accuracy
description: The cue-utilization framework (Brunswik; Koriat) holds that judgments are inferential: people use pieces of information, or cues, when making judgments, and judgment accuracy depends on how predictive, or diagnostic, those cues are of the judged outcome. For teacher judgments of student learning, cues are grouped into task cues, student cues, and performance cues, with performance cues generally correlating highest with student performance. This study experimentally tested the framework's central tenet for task-specific teacher judgments of text comprehension, manipulating cue availability and diagnosticity.
requirements: Cue diagnosticity must be determined by measuring cue values and calculating the correlation between cue value and performance on the judged task
constraints: Mnemonic cues are internal to the learner and typically not available to teachers, so the teacher-judgment variant uses task, student, and performance cues instead
target_learners: Secondary school teachers judging students' text comprehension
target_learning_goals: Accurate teacher judgment of students' text comprehension to support adaptive instruction
examples: In the experiment, diagnostic cues were the four most diagnostic performance cues from students' diagramming tasks (e.g., number of correct boxes, diagnosticity 0.63) and non-diagnostic cues included Dutch grade (0.03) and interest in the text topic (0.19)

description: The article frames monitoring judgments via cue-utilization theory (Koriat), in which confidence judgments are informed by information-based cues (beliefs about the self, cognition, and the task) and experience-based cues (e.g., solving speed, familiarity, feedback). The authors state that "The accuracy of judgments is dependent upon the validity of the cues that are used". The study applies this framework to health-related math problems, testing math self-efficacy and anxiety as information-based cues and worked-example training and accuracy as experience-based cues.

citation: Anja Prinz & Stefanie Golke & Jörg Wittwer. (2020). To What Extent Do Situation-Model-Approach Interventions Improve Relative Metacomprehension Accuracy? Meta-Analytic Insights. Educational Psychology Review (2020) 32:917–949. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09558-6
title: Taxonomy of situation-model interventions by cue-generation (encoding- vs retrieval-based), cue-attention, and cue-selection mechanisms
description: The article classifies the seven interventions by mechanism: self-explaining and concept mapping are encoding-based cue-generation interventions; delayed-summary writing, delayed-keywords listing, and delayed-diagram completion are retrieval-based cue-generation interventions; rereading is a cue-attention intervention; and comprehension-test expectancy is a cue-selection intervention. The distinction is empirically supported because effects of self-explaining were "nonoverlapping" with those of rereading and test expectancy. Delayed-generation tasks work because "performing a generation task after a delay allows for the surface and textbase representations to decay, forcing learners to access and use their situation model."
requirements: Delayed-generation tasks must be performed after a delay, after all texts are read, to be effective
Concept mapping requires extensive instruction and training before learners benefit
constraints: Delayed-generation benefits may not consistently occur for primary- and secondary-school students, depending on generation quality and cognitive capacity

university students

use of situation-model cues in self-assessment
