description: Because the article argues that academic self-concepts are culturally contingent, educators and researchers should consider whether explicit social and cultural supports for valuing academic competencies are present when explaining students' motivation. The article states these self-concepts' importance is "dependent on explicit social and cultural supports for their valuation", with "implications for understanding variation students’ relative valuation of academic competencies and their motivations to engage in academic learning".

constraints: The article offers this as a theoretical implication, not a tested intervention recommendation

article_title: The Relation Between Students’ Effort and Monitoring Judgments During Learning: A Meta-analysis
citation: Martine Baars & Lisette Wijnia & Anique de Bruin & Fred Paas. (2020). The Relation Between Students' Effort and Monitoring Judgments During Learning: A Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09569-3
title: Cue utilization perspective with data-driven versus goal-driven self-regulation as an account of effort-based monitoring
description: The article organizes its synthesis around the cue utilization perspective (Koriat 1997), in which monitoring judgments are inferential and learners use cues such as perceived invested effort. Under the memorizing effort heuristic, data-driven self-regulation in self-paced learning produces a negative effort–monitoring correlation, whereas goal-driven self-regulation (incentives, time pressure, self-agency) can reverse or nullify it. The meta-analysis provides evidence for both processes: "learners tend to focus on data-driven self-regulation in which monitoring judgments are based on the amoun t of effort that was needed to learn the study material".
requirements: Effort and monitoring must be measured in the same trial for the same item or criterion task for the association to be observed
constraints: A significant positive correlation under goal-driven regulation was not obtained in the moderator analyses
Some studies report an inverted U-shaped curvilinear relationship that neither data-driven nor goal-driven accounts alone explain
target_learners: learners across grades 1–6, grades 7–12, and higher education
target_learning_goals: accurate metacognitive monitoring during self-regulated learning
examples: The meta-analysis tested Hypothesis 1 (negative association) and Hypotheses 3a/3b (goal-driven manipulations) derived from this framework

citation: Avi Kaplan · Joanna K. Garner. (2026). A Complexity Perspective on Culture, Identity, and Motivation: The Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10221-9
title: Culture in the DSMRI as a complex, dynamic, symbolically mediated cultural activity system integrating four perspectives
description: The DSMRI conceptualizes the sociocultural facet of motivated action as a complex, dynamic, symbolically mediated cultural activity system that frames the emergence of individuals' role identities, motivation, and action. It integrates four complementary perspectives: Maehr's conception of culture as collective meaning-making in context, symbolic interactionism's symbolic social structures and role identities, conceptions of culture as itself a CDS reflecting self-organization, nonlinearity, and micro–macro influences, and Cultural-Historical Activity Theory as the framing structure. The article states the four perspectives "converge on culture as a shared, hierarchically structured, dynamic system of meanings." CHAT's third-generation model contributes the six interrelated elements—subject, object, tools, community, rules, and division of labor.
requirements: Requires treating culture as a comprehensive system of shared meanings rather than reducing it to variables, artifacts, or behavioral scripts
constraints: The article notes the culture concept has a long history of jingle-jangle ambiguity, with the same term used for different phenomena
target_learners: Participants in culturally situated educational activity systems
target_learning_goals: Explaining how cultural activity systems frame role identity emergence
examples: The article draws on Serpell's three metaphors of culture—Womb, Language, and Forum—arguing cultures manifest all three simultaneously

article_title: Towards a Comprehensive View of Object-Oriented Play
citation: Wynberg, E. R., Boland, A., Raijmakers, M. E. J., & van der Veen, C. (2021). Towards a Comprehensive View of Object-Oriented Play. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09608-7
title: Cultural historical psychological account of object-oriented play as mediated, socially embedded manipulative play
description: In cultural historical psychology, children's object manipulation is understood as child-caregiver joint object-centered activity and manipulative play, whose defining features are its associative nature and repetition. Development proceeds through leading activities: emotional interaction with caregivers in the first year, then manipulative play as the leading activity of the second and third years, followed by object substitution and sociodramatic play. The perspective emphasizes mediation: adults model procedures with psychological tools, which the child internalizes, and play "has the potential to create a zone of proximal development".
requirements: Children depend on their surroundings and caregiver mediation to discover the social meanings of objects
Adults must first model the procedure of object substitution for the child to acquire, master, and internalize it
constraints: The two types of manipulative thought (exploring characteristics without a practical goal and manipulating toward a practical goal) are described as not separable in their pure forms but closely interrelated
target_learners: children aged 1 to 3 years in joint activity with caregivers
target_learning_goals: speech development
symbolic thought
social-emotional stability
motor skills
communication skills
examples: In the bottle example, the educator models twisting off the top, involves Bobby by directing his attention, then withdraws until the procedure mediates his mental process.

article_title: How to Optimize Self-Assessment Accuracy in Cognitive Skill Acquisition When Learning from Worked Examples
citation: Waldeyer, J., Endres, T., Roelle, J., Baars, M., & Renkl, A. (2024). How to Optimize Self-Assessment Accuracy in Cognitive Skill Acquisition When Learning from Worked Examples. Educational Psychology Review, 36, 103. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09944-4
title: Cue-utilization framework of self-assessment
description: The article adopts the cue-utilization framework (attributed to Koriat) as its theoretical model of how learners form self-assessments and why these are often inaccurate. According to the article, "learners infer their self-assessments from cues, which they can monitor during learning", such as solution fluency, retrievability, or interest. Accuracy is thought to depend on how diagnostic the utilized cues are in the given context, so inaccurate self-assessments are assumed to result from monitoring cues of low diagnosticity. The study applies this framework by manipulating which cue learners are prompted to monitor during the initial problem-solving phase of worked-example learning.
requirements: Learners must be able to monitor the relevant cue during learning, as the framework assumes cues are monitored while learning proceeds.
constraints: The article notes the diagnosticity of a cue is context-dependent, so a cue that is diagnostic in one setting may be misleading in another, such as shallowly solved problems.
target_learners: university students in self-regulated example-based learning
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment of one's level of understanding during cognitive skill acquisition
examples: The experiments prompted learners to infer self-assessments either from how well they solved the four problems or from how well they could explain how the problems are solved.

article_title: The Role of Mental Effort in Fostering Self-Regulated Learning with Problem-Solving Tasks
citation: Tamara van Gog & Vincent Hoogerheide & Milou van Harsel. (2020). The Role of Mental Effort in Fostering Self-Regulated Learning with Problem-Solving Tasks. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09544-y
title: Cue-utilization framework: monitoring judgments rest on cues whose diagnosticity determines accuracy, with invested mental effort as a candidate cue
description: The cue-utilization framework (Koriat 1997), as applied in this review, holds that learners base monitoring judgments on sources of information (cues) arising from the study material and their studying experience, and that judgment accuracy depends on how predictive those cues are of actual test performance. The review uses it to explain why generative activities improve monitoring: they give learners access to cues about their understanding. It further develops an effort-as-cue account, noting that "Several studies have found students'effort ratings to correlate negatively with their monitoring judgments", while cautioning that effort is informative only when it reflects mental-model quality rather than extraneous processing or instructional support.
requirements: Effort ratings must be interpretable relative to the quality of the associated performance, and activity design must tie effort cues to mental-model quality rather than extraneous factors
constraints: Evidence that students use effort as a cue is correlational; effort ratings can be influenced by feedback valence and reporting timing, and students likely cannot distinguish the origin of invested effort
target_learners: secondary education students
higher education students learning problem-solving tasks
target_learning_goals: accurate self-monitoring of problem-solving performance
adaptive task selection in self-regulated learning
examples: The review interprets Baars et al. (2013): completion-condition students reported more effort and negatively correlated effort with judgments of learning, possibly using high effort as a cue for poor understanding

article_title: On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging
citation: Rebecca Covarrubias. (2024). On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09970-2
title: Taxonomy of cultural scripts of acceptance: sameness, difference, and pluralism
description: The article organizes institutional acceptance practices into three cultural scripts (Table 1). Scripts of acceptance through sameness require assimilation into dominant culture; scripts of acceptance through difference acknowledge cultural differences substantively via identity-conscious approaches such as culturally relevant cues and pedagogy; and scripts of acceptance through pluralism acknowledge the plurality of students' identities and interrogate the politics of belonging. Harmful scripts communicate a trade-off in which students must hide or contort parts of the self to be accepted, while pluralist scripts 'communicate how marginalized students need not trade important parts of themselves to be accepted.'
requirements: Scripts must be analyzed for whether they attend to the politics of belonging, not merely whether they signal acceptance
constraints: Culturally sustaining pedagogy reflects acceptance through pluralism but is organized under acceptance through difference in the main text to analyze similarities with culturally relevant pedagogy
target_learners: marginalized undergraduate students in universities
target_learning_goals: designing institutional practices that foster belonging without demanding assimilation
examples: Table 1 lists illustrative examples: multiculturalism and exceptionalism under sameness; culturally relevant cues and culturally relevant pedagogy under difference; culturally sustaining pedagogy and loving playfulness under pluralism
key_sources: Rebecca Covarrubias. (2024). On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09970-2

article_title: Homo Curious: Curious or Interested?
citation: Shin, D. D., & Kim, S. (2019). Homo Curious: Curious or Interested? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09497-x
title: Curiosity as an appetite-like drive to fill an information gap
description: The review develops an appetite analogy for curiosity: hunger is to appetite as uncertainty is to curiosity, so that "curiosity is a desire for information in order to reduce the psychological discomfort of uncertainty." Under drive theory, curiosity is a homeostatic state reduced by filling the information gap, which reinforces information-seeking. The review uses this account to explain why curiosity is aversive yet rewarding, and why information seeking follows a cost–benefit analysis.
requirements: A recognizable information gap between current and desired knowledge that the learner is aware of
constraints: The curiosity–uncertainty relationship is inverted U-shaped: too much information or too large a gap kills curiosity
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students
target_learning_goals: Information-seeking and knowledge acquisition driven by curiosity
key_sources: Shin, D. D., & Kim, S. (2019). Homo Curious: Curious or Interested? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09497-x

article_title: Mapping and Drawing to Improve Students’ and Teachers’ Monitoring and Regulation of Students’ Learning from Text: Current Findings and Future Directions
citation: Janneke van de Pol, et al. (2020). Mapping and Drawing to Improve Students’ and Teachers’ Monitoring and Regulation of Students’ Learning from Text: Current Findings and Future Directions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09560-y
title: Cue utilization framework for monitoring accuracy in learning from text
description: The review adopts the cue utilization framework (Koriat, 1997) as its organizing account of monitoring accuracy in learning from text. It holds that monitoring judgments depend on the cues people use, defined as "bits of information that might potentially be drawn upon or referred to [ … ] to inform a judgment." Cues diagnostic of students' text comprehension should be used and non-diagnostic cues ignored; students and teachers tend to use low-diagnosticity cues such as text length or effort, which harms accuracy. Generative activities like mapping and drawing make diagnostic cues available, and the framework underpins the review's analysis of cue diagnosticity and cue utilization.
requirements: Cues coded from generative-activity products must be reliably measurable so their relation to judgments (cue utilization) and to test performance (cue diagnosticity) can be determined
constraints: The framework is applied in this review to complex text comprehension tasks with mapping and drawing activities
target_learners: students learning from texts in primary, secondary, and university education
target_learning_goals: accurate monitoring and regulation of text comprehension
key_sources: Janneke van de Pol, et al. (2020). Mapping and Drawing to Improve Students’ and Teachers’ Monitoring and Regulation of Students’ Learning from Text: Current Findings and Future Directions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09560-y

article_title: What Makes Learners Overestimate Their Text Comprehension? The Impact of Learner Characteristics on Judgment Bias
citation: Stefanie Golke, Tim Steininger, & Jörg Wittwer. (2022). What Makes Learners Overestimate Their Text Comprehension? The Impact of Learner Characteristics on Judgment Bias. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09687-0
title: Cue-utilization framework extended to learner characteristics as sources of judgment bias in metacomprehension
description: The article organizes its predictions with the cue-utilization framework (Koriat, 1997), in which metacomprehension accuracy depends on the cues learners use to infer comprehension because "cues differ in their validity in indicating actual understanding." Representation-based cues emerge from monitoring text processing and are rather valid; heuristic cues such as self-perceptions of ability are available whether or not a text has been read and are usually less valid. The study extends this account by treating learner characteristics as sources of these cues and argues such characteristics "should be incorporated explicitly in theories of judgment accuracy."
requirements: Learners make comprehension judgments before and/or after answering comprehension questions, providing judgment-bias measures
constraints: The article notes which characteristics impact judgment bias also depends on task requirements, such as factual versus inference questions
target_learners: university students reading expository texts
target_learning_goals: accurate monitoring and judgment of one's own text comprehension
examples: The study assessed 255 university students' predictions and postdictions for factual and inference questions on three expository texts and regressed judgment bias on cognitive, metacognitive, motivational, and personality characteristics simultaneously
key_sources: Stefanie Golke, Tim Steininger, & Jörg Wittwer. (2022). What Makes Learners Overestimate Their Text Comprehension? The Impact of Learner Characteristics on Judgment Bias. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09687-0

article_title: The Relation Between Perceived Mental Effort, Monitoring Judgments, and Learning Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Louise David, Felicitas Biwer, Martine Baars, Lisette Wijnia, Fred Paas, Anique de Bruin. (2024). The Relation Between Perceived Mental Effort, Monitoring Judgments, and Learning Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09903-z
title: Cue-utilization framework for metacognitive monitoring in self-regulated learning
description: The framework holds that learners who cannot access their learning outcomes directly infer them from indirect cues arising from study experiences or materials, such as processing fluency or perceived mental effort. The article states that "three elements are involved in self-regulated learning: cues, monitoring judgments, and actual learning or performance". Cue diagnosticity is the extent to which cues predict outcomes, and monitoring accuracy is the extent to which judgments predict outcomes. The article operationalizes this triangle in its MASEM with perceived mental effort as cue, monitoring judgments as mediator, and learning outcomes as performance approximation.
requirements: Cues, monitoring judgments, and learning outcomes must be measured in the same study or experiment on the same task for the triangular relationships to be estimated
constraints: Often learners utilize cues that are not diagnostic of actual learning outcomes, which the article states leads to inaccurate monitoring
target_learners: learners across education levels, from primary grades to postgraduate education
target_learning_goals: accurate metacognitive monitoring of learning during self-regulated learning
examples: The article specified perceived mental effort as the cue, monitoring judgments as the mediator, and learning outcomes as the outcome in its full mediation MASEM

article_title: Critical culturalized comprehension: Exploring culture as learners thinking about texts
citation: Alexandra List, Gala S. Campos Oaxaca, Hongcui Du, Hye Yeon Lee, Bailing Lyu. (2023). Critical culturalized comprehension: exploring culture as learners thinking about texts. Educational Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2023.2266028
title: Culturalized comprehension: culture as a way of thinking about texts, not an individual difference
description: The article proposes culturalized comprehension as a framework in which culture is conceptualized as a way of thinking rather than an individual difference factor. It defines it as "individuals' reasoning about the commonalities and differences in their and others' worldviews and the linking of these to underlying values". When this reasoning is engaged in reference to texts, the article names it culturalized comprehension, positioning it as an extension of comprehension theories centered on cognitive representation of texts.
requirements: Learners must engage in reasoning that links commonalities and differences across their own and others' worldviews to underlying values.
constraints: The framework applies when such worldview reasoning is engaged in reference to texts, as the article states.
target_learners: readers in educational psychology research contexts
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
critical reasoning about texts

article_title: The role of authoritative and authoritarian parenting in the early academic achievement of Latino students.
citation: Kim Yeonwoo, Calzada Esther J., Barajas-Gonzalez R. Gabriela, Huang Keng-Yen, Brotman Laurie M., Castro Ashley, Pichardo Catherine. (2018). The Role of Authoritative and Authoritarian Parenting in the Early Academic Achievement of Latino Students. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000192
title: Cultural framework of Latino parenting and student academic achievement
description: The article tests a cultural framework (Calzada, Fernandez, & Cortes, 2010; Figure 1) in which "mothers' acculturative status is expected to influence socialization messages of respeto or independence and the authoritarian or authoritative parenting practices that reinforce them; both, in turn, are expected to influence child developmental outcomes." Cultural socialization is the process through which parents transmit cultural values, beliefs, traditions, and behavioral norms. The framework was tested with multi-group SEM, separately for Mexican and Dominican American families, with school readiness (academic and social-emotional) as the mediator between parenting and first-grade achievement.

constraints: The framework was tested with cross-sectional data for the acculturation-to-parenting-readiness paths, so temporal ordering and causality cannot be inferred
Findings cannot be generalized to Latino families beyond Mexican and Dominican origin

target_learning_goals: Early academic achievement
Social-emotional school readiness

article_title: Adolescent well-being and school engagement as a function of teacher and peer relatedness: The more (relatedness) is not always the merrier.
citation: Núñez-Regueiro, F., & Wang, M.-T. (2024). Adolescent Well-Being and School Engagement as a Function of Teacher and Peer Relatedness: The More (Relatedness) Is Not Always the Merrier. Journal of Educational Psychology, 117(3), 466-484. https://hal.science/hal-04920252v1
title: Complex social ecology of school relatedness operationalized through cubic response surface analysis with five congruence hypotheses
description: The article extends the complex social ecology model, which conceptualizes the "collective influences" that social partners may have on youth development, by operationalizing collective effects of peer and teacher relatedness with cubic polynomial regression. Its cubic RSA uses a model "composed of 9 regression parameters" whose constraints instantiate five congruence hypotheses (cumulative coaction, interdependent needs, peer-specific, teacher-specific, and complete compensatory processes), tested in Study 1 and cross-validated in Study 2 with alternative measures. The approach mixes variable-centered predictive effects with person-centered typological patterns along the lines of congruence and incongruence.
requirements: Commensurable, standardized predictors and outcomes so response surfaces along the LOC and LOIC can be interpreted
Sufficient sample and measures of both relatedness sources and the outcome to fit and compare constrained polynomial families
constraints: In Study 1, data clustering could not be modeled because student class membership was unknown
RSA had never been applied in this context, so unexpected congruence processes could fit better than the five hypotheses
target_learners: adolescents in secondary school
target_learning_goals: student well-being
school engagement
examples: Study 1 fit a congruence-effect family to well-being (R2 = .171) and an asymmetric congruence family to engagement (R2 = .284), selected via absolute fit, AIC/BIC weights, and 1000 bootstrapped samples.

article_title: Cues to generality: Integrating linguistic and visual information when generalizing biological information.
citation: David Menendez. (2023). Cues to generality: Integrating linguistic and visual information when generalizing biological information. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000812
title: Cues to generality hypothesis
description: The cues to generality hypothesis is the article's proposed account of "how students use information in lessons to determine how far to generalize." It holds that learners treat features of both the linguistic and visual modalities — such as generic noun phrases and perceptual richness — as cues signaling whether a taught fact applies narrowly or broadly, and integrate these cues when deciding how far to extend the information to untaught exemplars. The eight studies substantiate it by showing that text-type cues operate similarly across ages, while the weight given to visual cues changes with development and with whether visual attention is split between text and image.
requirements: Lessons must present information in both linguistic and visual modalities for the cue-integration account to apply
constraints: The account was developed from studies of animal-fact generalization with undergraduate and elementary-school participants; the author notes the advantage of bland visualizations is context dependent, varying with task and learner
target_learners: undergraduate students
elementary school students in grades 1-5
target_learning_goals: generalizing biological facts from multimedia lessons to untaught category members
examples: In Study 8, children generalized most when the text was generic and the visualization was rich, the most common text-image combination found in the elementary science books analyzed in Study 1
key_sources: David Menendez. (2023). Cues to generality: Integrating linguistic and visual information when generalizing biological information. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000812

title: Cultural variation account of the growth mindset framework
description: The article proposes that the growth mindset of intelligence is culturally ingrained rather than universal: it argues that "the growth mindset of intelligence is not a universal belief system that uniformly characterizes individuals' motivation to learn and predicts academic achievement". The account unifies prior null and negative findings in non-WEIRD samples (e.g. Chinese students' "fixed mindset, high performer" pattern) with the stronger mindset–achievement links observed in WEIRD countries, using Cultural and Psychological Distance from the US as the organizing axis.

target_learning_goals: Academic motivation and beliefs about the malleability of intelligence

citation: Long, Y., Luo, H. & Zhang, Y. (2024). Evaluating large language models in analysing classroom dialogue. npj Science of Learning 9:60. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00273-3

description: The authors built a customised GPTs application (OpenAI's "My GPTs") that codes classroom dialogue automatically. citation: Avia Ben-Ari, Tess Gavrielle Levinson, Jessica Blake-West, Marina Umaschi Bers, Rinat B. Rosenberg-Kima. (2025). From avoidance to ownership: preschool teachers learn to teach code—a case study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10548-0
title: Invite teachers to critically adapt a new curriculum and provide accessible support, since agency plus support can dismantle resistance even after brief training
description: The article finds that inviting teachers to adjust a new curriculum where they believe needed, while requiring each modification to be articulated and justified to a research team, helped dismantle initial resistance and fostered ownership. The teachers agreed that "the training [they] went through helped [dismantle] pressure", and the authors argue that being invited to critically engage with the curriculum facilitated an emotional connection with it, enabling continuous curricular involvement and adaptation.

Modifications are reviewed and approved rather than made in isolation

description: The commentary advances the view that design principles which appear universal, such as owning, learning, and sharing knowledge, carry culture-dependent meanings. It states that "owning, learning, and sharing are principles that can be appreciated by systems of education around the globe," yet their "definitions and understandings" must be reconsidered across cultures. article_title: Invisible borders in educational technology research? A comparative analysis
citation: Marín, V. I., Buntins, K., Bedenlier, S., & Bond, M. (2023). Invisible borders in educational technology research? A comparative analysis. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10195-3
title: Cultural clusters and national research traditions as an explanatory framework for EdTech research topics
description: The article frames country differences in EdTech research using Ronen and Shenkar's eco-cultural clustering, which "consider[s] three main variables (religion, language and geography)" and identifies 11 global clusters, with Germany in the Germanic, Spain in the Latin European and the UK in the Anglo cluster. It layers this over Biesta's distinction between the Anglo-Saxon tradition from curriculum studies and the continental tradition from Pädagogik, attributing Germany and Spain to the continental tradition and the UK to the Anglo-Saxon tradition. The framework explains why topical clusters persist despite a shared publication language.
requirements: Research traditions and cultural cluster membership must be considered when comparing EdTech research across countries
constraints: The article notes the three clusters are similar in economic terms (high GDP-PPP), so economic aspects may influence EdTech research development and were not closely considered in the study
target_learners: Educational technology researchers
Comparative education scholars
target_learning_goals: Understanding how national research traditions shape EdTech research topics and terminology
examples: Germany's Medienpädagogik divided into Medienerziehung and Mediendidaktik; Spain's Tecnología Educativa framed within Didáctica; the UK's shift toward technology enhanced learning as lingua franca

citation: Neslihan Yondemir Çalişkan, Emine Şendurur. (2025). The effect of cumulative eye movements' guidance of experts on transition from novice to expert. Education Tech Research Dev, 73:59–89. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10414-5

description: Eight weekly instructional videos built from the cumulative eye movements of seven professional graphic-designer experts, plus screen, voice, and mouse recordings. Unlike most prior EMME work using one expert, seven experts' fixations were cumulatively ranked on AOIs to decide when signals appeared.

Video production aligned with multimedia design principles and cognitive load theory guidelines
constraints: Participants were not informed of the roots or aims of the provided signals
The intervention ran weekly over eight weeks, longer than typical one-shot EMME studies

target_learning_goals: procedural use of Adobe Photoshop tools and interface
examples: Week 1 introduced the workspace and experts' fixations were heavily located within the toolbox AOI, so a red rectangular frame frequently appeared around the toolbox as a signal

article_title: Very short answer questions vs. multiple choice questions in health professions education: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Sher Ali, Arshad Muhammad Moin Ud Din, Abbas Mesum, Asghar Abdul Hannan, Khan Anees Hussain, Ali Junaid, Yaqoob Muhammad Ibrahim, Alam Rana Aftab, Akram Muhammad Bilal, Masood Muhammad Abdullah, Thakur Amit Kumar. (2026). Very short answer questions vs. multiple choice questions in health professions education: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09359-5
title: Cueing-effect account: MCQ recognition inflates scores while VSAQs require self-generated responses reflecting independent knowledge
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that MCQs are "susceptible to cueing effects, where recognition rather than recall may drive performance, potentially inflating student scores without truly reflecting independent knowledge". VSAQs mitigate this by requiring concise, self-generated responses of 1-4 words while retaining computer-markable logistics. The review uses this account to interpret lower VSAQ scores as more authentic assessment of independent knowledge and clinical reasoning rather than a learning deficiency.
requirements: VSAQs must be computer-markable with a limited word count (1-4 words) to retain logistical feasibility
constraints: Both formats require retrieval from memory; the principal distinction is that VSAQs reduce response cueing and place greater demands on answer generation
target_learners: undergraduate and postgraduate health professions education students
target_learning_goals: assessment of independent knowledge and clinical reasoning ability
examples: The review interprets the pooled score difference favoring MCQs as consistent with recognition-driven answering inflating MCQ scores, citing prior literature on MCQ overestimation of mastery.

citation: MacLean Tammy L., Qiang Jinfan Rose, Henderson Lynn, Bowra Andrea, Howard Lisa, Pringle Victoria, Butsang Tenzin, Rice Emma, Di Ruggiero Erica, Mashford-Pringle Angela. (2023). Indigenous Cultural Safety Training for Applied Health, Social Work, and Education Professionals: A PRISMA Scoping Review. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph20065217
title: Cultural safety and related concepts form a contested conceptual landscape with distinct geopolitical origins, often used interchangeably and rarely critiqued
description: The review describes a family of overlapping concepts — cultural safety, cultural competence, cultural sensitivity, cultural responsiveness, cultural knowledge, cultural awareness, and cultural humility — that emerged from the included studies and were "often used interchangeably". It traces two concepts' origins: cultural safety emerged in New Zealand via a Māori nurse working within the health system, while cultural competence developed in the United States within the transcultural nursing movement. It highlights Baba's 2013 report distinguishing cultural safety, cultural competence, cultural awareness, and cultural sensitivity as a resource for consolidating terms. The review uses this landscape to argue the field needs conceptual clarity about which concepts are preferable in which contexts.
requirements: Concepts should be justified and clearly cited when chosen, and applied with attention to the socio-political and historical contexts in which they emerged
constraints: Only half of selected papers described or cited a cultural safety or similar concept, and less than a fifth provided a critique of one
target_learners: health, social work, and education professionals and students undertaking cultural safety training
target_learning_goals: understanding cultural safety and related concepts and their appropriate application in professional practice
examples: The review's Table 3 outlines definitions of cultural safety, cultural competence, cultural awareness, and cultural sensitivity drawn from Baba's 2013 report

citation: Stephen Gorard, Nadia Siddiqui, Beng Huat See, Emma Smith, Patrick White. (2017). Children's University: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation.
title: Children's University Passport to Learning credit and certification system
description: The Passport to Learning is each pupil's logbook (booklet and online version) recording every CU-validated activity and hours spent on it. Hours spent on approved learning activities are rewarded by collecting credits that lead to certificates, from Bronze Undergraduate Award level at 30 hours to Gold Fellowship level at 1,000 hours. Children choose their own activities and receive a stamp upon completion, and teachers log participation after training in the reward credit system. Completion of 30 hours earns certification and participation in a graduation ceremony attended by parents.

constraints: Final credits and certification depend on the records of pupils' Passports to Learning, so record-keeping by trained teachers is integral to the reward system

target_learning_goals: Motivating participation in informal out-of-school learning
Recording and rewarding hours of learning activity
examples: In the trial, teachers logged pupils' participation and hours in Passports to Learning after CU training, and CU managers monitored execution of activities through regular visits

Innovative ways of learning connecting out-of-school opportunities with classroom learning

description: The article applies cumulative sum (CUSUM) methods as a quantitative framework for defining surgical proficiency. For a binary outcome, CUSUM(i) = CUSUM(i − 1) + [X(i) – p0], where the curve peak "identifies the proficiency point, i.e. the case after which performance was consistently better than the cohort average"; for operative time the trough marks the inflection. surgical educators and credentialing bodies

title: Cue-utilisation framework for self-monitoring accuracy
description: The article draws on the cue-utilisation framework put forward by Koriat to explain differences in self-monitoring accuracy between studies. article_title: Application of CUSUM analysis in assessing learning curves in robot-assisted sacrocolpopexy performed by experienced gynecologist.
citation: Park Kena, Kwon Ji Young, Yoo Eun-Hee, Lee Seon Hwa, Song Jeong Min, Pyeon Seung Yeon. (2024). Application of CUSUM analysis in assessing learning curves in robot-assisted sacrocolpopexy performed by experienced gynecologist. BMC Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12893-024-02691-x
title: CUSUM analysis with piecewise linear regression as a method for mapping surgical learning curves
description: Cumulative sum (CUSUM) analysis, originally developed for quality control in manufacturing, computes the running sum of deviations of each case's operative time from the mean, so that a downward slope indicates a shorter-than-expected operation time and an upward slope a longer-than-expected one. The article applies it to a chronological series of robot-assisted sacrocolpopexies and uses piecewise linear regression to locate breakpoints separating Learning, Proficiency, and Competency phases. The authors state it is "able to detect even the subtle shifts in parameters of any given procedure" and can "allow real-time monitoring of surgeon proficiency and competency by detecting fine patterns after controlling for random variations".
requirements: A chronological series of consecutive cases with a defined performance parameter such as total operative time, and piecewise linear regression to identify phase breakpoints
constraints: CUSUM is primarily effective for merely detecting trends and shifts in performance without the ability to provide insights into the underlying reason for changes such as patient selection, trainee involvement or concomitant procedures
Risk-adjusted CUSUM analysis may be needed to compensate for CUSUM's inability to account for variability in case complexity
target_learners: experienced surgeons transitioning to a new robotic technique
surgical trainees and training-program designers
target_learning_goals: acquisition of proficiency and competency in a new surgical technique
examples: The study computed CUSUM of operative time for 50 consecutive robot-assisted sacrocolpopexies and fitted a broken-line model, identifying breakpoints at cases 9 and 35

title: CUSUM chart with first-peak convention for charting surgical learning curves
